lines.say: One short beep. That's the letter E. And it's where this whole thing started.
I'm learning to sail here in Turkey. My course needs an amateur radio certificate, and for that, I had to learn Morse code.
So I did what everyone does. I opened the chart and started memorising. A: dot dash. B: dash dot dot dot.
It didn't stick. I'd hear a beep, picture the dots, then go looking for the letter. Way too slow.
What finally worked was learning each letter by its sound. Shortest ones first, at full speed, with room to think in between.
So I turned that method into an app. It's called MorseForge, and the front page is your first lesson. Tap once, and you've sent an E.
Every letter, you see it, you hear it, then you send it back yourself. Two letters on day one, all of them by day seven.
The Signal Tree shows why each letter sounds the way it does: a dot goes one way, a dash the other.
Your keyboard becomes a telegraph key. Try sending SOS.
The games only count if you really know the code. Reading the screen won't save you.
There's a daily challenge, the same for everyone, and your result shares without spoiling it.
Or send a friend your sixty-second test: same letters, same order, same speed.
You can even send a secret message that only plays in Morse.
And if you can't use sound, switch to the lamp, and learn it by light.
It's free. No account, nothing to install, and it works offline.
I'm still learning too. Come learn with me. MorseForge.
